paras: The attempted lynching of Dick Thompson took place in Centralia, Missouri, on a Tuesday night in November 1903, when a crowd of about two hundred men gathered at the city hall where Thompson, a Black man accused of indecent conduct before schoolgirls, was being held. Officers and deputized citizens guarded him through the night, and he was afterward fined $100 and costs in a justice court. Two weeklies in Mexico, Missouri, reported the episode under the headlines "Lynching Averted" and "Almost a Lynching."

Thompson, described as "a negro," was arrested on a Tuesday evening, accused of "indecent conduct before some little girls" or, in the Mexico Weekly Ledger's wording, indecent exposure before school girls. According to the Centralia Guard, as soon as it became known that he was in the city hall, about two hundred men gathered around the building, threats were made of taking him out and whipping him, and "an omnious looking rope" was dragged about the park. The Ledger said that only "the interference of some" kept him from being "handled with violence."

The Guard stressed that no demand was made on the city officers to surrender him, though men posted on all sides would not let him be moved, and the officers deputized citizens and kept him under guard all night. Most of the crowd dispersed around midnight, but small groups watched the roads from the park until daybreak. Once the morning train for Columbia had left, the citizens and the officers inside relaxed the guard.

When the train returned with Sheriff Bradford and Prosecuting Attorney Harris, the crowd gathered again and word spread that Thompson was gone. The crowd rushed the hall and searched it, then rushed to the livery stable, and mounted men rode out in all directions. W. C. Acuff and Vaughn Hulen, riding east to the town of Thompson, met him coming in, and he agreed to return with them; he said that someone had come into his room at the city hall and told him to escape.

Thompson was brought back and tried before Justice Boyd, who fined him $100 and costs. The Ledger reported that he was jailed in default of payment, while the Guard said he was sent at once to Columbia in a buggy. No report names anyone in the crowd or any action taken against it.

Both known reports appeared on 12 November 1903 on the front pages of two weeklies in Mexico, Missouri. The Mexico Weekly Ledger ran a short item headed "Lynching Averted," describing Centralia people as "wrought to a frenzy" over the accusation. The Mexico Missouri Message reprinted the Centralia Guard's long narrative under "AFTER HIM. Almost a Lynching--Negro Ran to Thompson," introducing it as showing "how near that town came to having a lynching."

Both accounts referred to Thompson mainly as "the negro" and reported the accusation as the cause of the crowd without questioning it. The Guard's version described the rope and the night-long watch without comment on the crowd, and it presented the pursuit as a chase after a fleeing prisoner, mentioning only in passing his statement that someone had told him to leave. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Dick Thompson
bases: A crowd of about two hundred men besieged the city hall where an accused Black man was held, threatening to take him out and whip him while a rope was dragged about, and both headlines called it a near lynching (A1, A2).

No one was killed: Thompson was guarded overnight, recaptured after leaving the building, fined in a justice court and sent to Columbia (A1, A2); the crowd of about two hundred acted without authority on an accusation of indecent conduct, so this was an attempted or threatened lynching, not a completed one (A2).
Two Mexico, Missouri weeklies with differently worded accounts, one a reprint of the Centralia Guard, agree on the arrest, the crowd at the jail, and the $100 fine before Justice Boyd (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Centralia Guard (local weekly), reprinted
accounts.gist: A crowd of about two hundred threatened to take Thompson out and whip him but made no demand on the officers; after the guard relaxed he was found gone, said someone had told him to escape, was met coming back at Thompson, tried, fined and sent to Columbia.

accounts.label: Mexico Weekly Ledger brief
accounts.gist: Centralia people were 'wrought to a frenzy'; only the interference of some kept the crowd from violence; Thompson was fined $100 and costs and jailed in default.

framing.detail: The Ledger headed its brief 'Lynching Averted' and named no one who interfered or who was in the crowd, reporting the accusation as the cause of the 'frenzy'.

The Message's 'AFTER HIM. Almost a Lynching--Negro Ran to Thompson' reprinted the Centralia Guard's narrative, which describes the 'omnious looking rope' and the crowd's watch without censure, stresses that no demand was made on the officers, and treats the chase as a story of the man's flight.

A large crowd of citizens gathered about the city jail and only for the interference of some the negro would have been handled with violence.
